This prolonged developmental phase is among the longest documented for any freshwater fish of comparable adult size. This initial mass is consistent with the production of relatively large, nutrient-rich eggs that sustain the endotrophic larva through its extended yolk-sac stage. The energetic investment per offspring is considerable, a pattern commonly interpreted as an adaptation to the resource-limited and stable thermal regime of the cave ecosystem, where high fecundity is not favoured.

This comparatively late maturation is a common life-history strategy among stygobitic fishes, likely driven by the low and unpredictable food availability in deep cave systems.

The rate of reproduction is therefore highly constrained, and population turnover is consequently very slow, which makes the species particularly vulnerable to any disturbance that increases adult mortality.
